Quote sources

Zhuangzi quote sources

10 passages attributed to Zhuangzi in this archive, each with the locator that lets you find it in the work itself — and the one thing that most often goes wrong when people quote Zhuangzi.

Quote source / Zhuangzi

How to cite this author, and what circulates under the name that is not theirs to give.

Sourcing profile

Language of the works
Classical Chinese
Cited here from
The Zhuangzi — the Inner Chapters (Free and Easy Wandering, Discussion on Making All Things Equal, The Primacy of Nourishing Life, The Great Ancestral Teacher) and chapters from the Outer and Miscellaneous books.
How to cite it
Give the Chinese chapter number as well as the translated title. Chapter names vary wildly between translators — the same book is “Qiwulun,” “Discussion on Making All Things Equal,” and “On the Equality of Things” — so the number is the only stable identifier.
Where quotations of this author go wrong
The received text has thirty-three chapters in Guo Xiang's fourth-century recension, and only the first seven, the Inner Chapters, have a strong claim to a single hand. Quoting from the Outer Chapters as the words of Zhuangzi assigns to one person material that most scholars treat as later work in his tradition.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I check quotations attributed to Zhuangzi?

Give the Chinese chapter number as well as the translated title. Chapter names vary wildly between translators — the same book is “Qiwulun,” “Discussion on Making All Things Equal,” and “On the Equality of Things” — so the number is the only stable identifier. This archive cites Zhuangzi from The Zhuangzi — the Inner Chapters (Free and Easy Wandering, Discussion on Making All Things Equal, The Primacy of Nourishing Life, The Great Ancestral Teacher) and chapters from the Outer and Miscellaneous books. Every passage listed on this page carries that locator, so it can be found in any edition of the work.

What is the most common mistake when quoting Zhuangzi?

The received text has thirty-three chapters in Guo Xiang's fourth-century recension, and only the first seven, the Inner Chapters, have a strong claim to a single hand. Quoting from the Outer Chapters as the words of Zhuangzi assigns to one person material that most scholars treat as later work in his tradition.

What language did Zhuangzi write in?

Classical Chinese. Any English sentence you read is a translation, so a complete source names the translator as well as the passage.
